lead: A DC machine is one device with two jobs. Spin it and it generates a DC voltage; feed it DC and it produces torque. The same parts do both: a field winding makes flux, a rotating armature carries conductors, and a commutator with brushes turns the coil's alternating EMF into direct voltage at the terminals. A motor's own rotation creates a back EMF that sets its current and torque. Shunt machines hold speed; series machines give high starting torque for traction and cranes.
prereq: You need: magnetic circuits for the field path, Faraday's law for the generated EMF, and KVL from Unit 1.

sections.h3: Construction: the parts that make a DC machine

blocks.text: A DC machine has a stationary field and a rotating armature. The yoke is a cast-iron or steel ring. It carries the magnetic flux from pole to pole and holds the machine together. Field poles are bolted inside the yoke. Each pole carries a field winding. When DC flows in the field winding, it sets up flux Φ per pole, as in magnetic circuits.
The armature is a laminated steel core with slots. Insulated conductors sit in the slots and form the armature winding. Laminations reduce eddy-current loss. The armature is the rotor.

The commutator is a ring of copper segments on the shaft, insulated from each other. Carbon brushes press on the segments and connect the rotating winding to the outside circuit. The commutator is a mechanical rectifier: it reverses the connection of each coil twice per revolution, so the coil's alternating EMF appears as direct voltage between the brushes. The brushes are stationary; the segments rotate.

sections.h3: Generator action: rotation makes DC at the terminals

blocks.text: Faraday's law says a conductor cutting flux gets an EMF. In a DC generator the prime mover turns the armature. Each conductor slides past the north pole and then the south pole, so the EMF in a single coil reverses every half turn. The commutator swaps the coil's terminals at the same instant, so the brush marked positive always touches the conductor under the north pole. The terminal voltage is unidirectional, though it ripples slightly. More coils and segments make the ripple small.

blocks.where: E is the generated EMF in volts; P is the number of poles; Φ is the flux per pole in webers; N is the speed in revolutions per minute; Z is the total number of armature conductors; A is the number of parallel paths in the armature winding. The 60 converts minutes to seconds.

blocks.text: A depends only on the winding. In lap winding the coils are connected so that each pole has its own parallel path: A = P. In wave winding the coils are connected in a single wave that always gives two parallel paths: A = 2, whatever the pole count. Lap winding suits low voltage and high current. Wave winding suits higher voltage and lower current.

sections.h3: Motor action: back EMF limits the current

blocks.text: Connect DC to the field and to the armature. Current in the armature conductors sits in the field's magnetic field, so each conductor feels a force F = BIl. The forces on the two sides of a coil form a torque, and the armature turns. This is motor action.

As soon as the armature turns, its conductors cut the same flux, so they generate an EMF. By Lenz's law this EMF opposes the supply. It is called the back EMF E_b. KVL around the armature gives V = E_b + I_aR_a, so I_a = (V − E_b)/R_a. At standstill E_b = 0 and the current is limited only by R_a, which is small. A starter resistance limits this starting current.

blocks.where: T is the torque in newton-metres; I_a is the armature current in amperes; P, Φ, Z and A are as in the EMF equation.

blocks.text: Torque rises with flux and with armature current. The motor is self-regulating: add load, speed dips, E_b falls, I_a rises, torque rises to match the load.

items: Separately excited: field from a separate DC supply.
Shunt: field winding in parallel with the armature; flux is almost constant, so speed is nearly constant from no load to full load.
Series: field winding in series with the armature; flux rises with current, giving very high starting torque; speed falls sharply with load, and the motor must never be run unloaded.
Compound: both shunt and series windings, a compromise between the two.

blocks.text: Uses: a shunt generator charges batteries and feeds lighting; a shunt motor drives lathes and fans; a series motor drives trains, cranes and lifts; a compound motor drives rolling mills and presses.

spec.title: Motor: back EMF sets the current
spec.aria: A 230 V supply drives the field and armature, the rotating armature generates 220 V back EMF, and the remaining 10 V drives 20 A to produce shaft torque against the load.

examples.question: A 4-pole lap-wound DC generator has 400 armature conductors, flux 0.03 Wb per pole and runs at 1500 rpm. Find the generated EMF. The same machine runs as a motor from 230 V, draws 20 A, and its armature resistance is 0.5 Ω; find the back EMF.
steps: Data: P = 4 poles, Φ = 0.03 Wb, N = 1500 rpm, Z = 400 conductors. Lap winding, so A = P = 4.
The 4 in the numerator cancels the 4 in the denominator: E = (0.03 × 1500 × 400) ÷ 60.
examples.answer: Generated EMF = 300 V; back EMF as a motor = 220 V.
examples.check:
P = 4
Phi = 0.03
N = 1500
Z = 400
A = P
E = P * Phi * N * Z / (60 * A)
print(E)
V = 230
Ia = 20
Ra = 0.5
Eb = V - Ia * Ra
print(Eb)

traps: Using A = 2 for a lap winding, or A = P for a wave winding. In lap A = P; in wave A = 2 always.
Putting N in rad/s in E = PΦNZ/(60A). The 60 assumes N in rpm.
Confusing generated EMF E with terminal voltage. In a generator V = E − I_aR_a; in a motor E_b = V − I_aR_a.
Thinking the back EMF is a separate battery. It is induced in the same armature conductors that carry the current.
Running a series motor at no load. With tiny flux the speed can rise to a dangerous value.

quiz.q: Name the main parts of a DC machine and state the job of the commutator.
quiz.a: Yoke, field poles with field winding, armature with winding, commutator, brushes. The commutator reverses each coil's connections twice per revolution so the coil's alternating EMF becomes direct voltage at the brushes.

quiz.q: Why is the back EMF called back EMF, and what happens to armature current when the load increases?
quiz.a: It opposes the supply voltage, as Lenz's law requires. When load increases, speed falls, so E_b falls and I_a = (V − E_b)/R_a rises, giving more torque.

quiz.q: A 4-pole wave-wound generator has 500 armature conductors, flux 0.02 Wb per pole and runs at 1200 rpm. Find the generated EMF.
A 220 V shunt motor has armature resistance 0.4 Ω and draws an armature current of 25 A. Find the back EMF.
Why must a series motor never be started without a load?
quiz.a: At no load the torque needed is tiny, so I_a is small and the series field gives small flux. Speed rises until E_b is almost equal to V; with small Φ the speed becomes dangerously high and the armature can be damaged.

quiz.q: Why is lap winding chosen for a low-voltage, high-current generator?
quiz.a: Lap gives A = P parallel paths, so each path carries only 1/P of the total current and the voltage per path is lower. The machine can supply a large current at low voltage without overheating the winding.

quiz.q: Write the EMF equation of a DC machine and state A for lap and wave windings.
quiz.a: E = PΦNZ/(60A). For lap, A = P; for wave, A = 2.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real DC machines need careful commutation design and interpoles to stop sparking at the brushes. Armature reaction shifts the magnetic neutral axis, and compensating windings correct it. In industry, DC drives are being replaced by BLDC and PMSM drives with electronic commutation — see the special machines chapter. Search for 'DC machine armature reaction' and 'back EMF motor control'.
